title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
description: This photo combination shows Reinaldo De
body:
This photo combination shows Reinaldo Dennes, left, on April 14, 2026 and Thomas Mitchell Overton.
                
                    Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP
    

   
   HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.   And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.   The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.   
   Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.   Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"   Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."   Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."   After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.   
   The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.   Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.   She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.   Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.   Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."   "This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.   Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.   "David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."   Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.   Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."   Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.   
   DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.   Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.   The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

title: Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
description: NEW ALBANY, OHIO - NOVEMBER 1: In an aer
body:
NEW ALBANY, OHIO - NOVEMBER 1: In an aerial view, a portion of the Meta Prometheus Campus, an AI data center and supercluster project, is seen on November 1, 2026 in New Albany, Ohio.
                
                    Jon Cherry/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jon Cherry/Getty Images
    

   
   As Americans struggle with rising energy costs and increased demand driven by artificial intelligence, the Senate on Thursday passed a bipartisan bill that will speed up the approval process for data centers and power plants.   
   The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, passed 62-33. Fourteen Democrats and one Independent joined most Republicans in supporting the bill. It now heads to the House. The bill was authored by two Democrats and two Republicans.   "Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people," said one of the bill's co-authors, West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito.   Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the bill would "cut through decades of red tape" and "save the average household hundreds of dollars each year, and Americans will see better roads, more American manufacturing, and better-paying jobs."   
   Rhode Island Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, who co-authored the bill, said "Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit."   
   Nationwide, the cost of a kilowatt-hour has risen faster than overall inflation: more than 6% in the last year and 39% in the last five years.   Whitehouse also said the bill would make data centers pay for the power they use. There has been considerable pushback by the public against data centers in the U.S., cutting across party lines.   Some climate change advocates say the U.S. needs to speed up building renewable energy projects and transmission lines and argue that the bill will allow the country to build more solar, wind and battery projects.   But major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have opposed the bill, arguing it will weaken environmental accountability.   Many Democrats have also opposed the bill. They say it will worsen pollution by making it easier to greenlight oil and gas projects and energy-hungry data centers, while weakening protections for clean air and water.   
   There is also concern the bill could undermine tribal rights.   "Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act, hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty," said Washington Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell on X.   California Sen. Alex Padilla had similar concerns. "I support cutting red tape and getting more energy projects built, but not at the expense of tribal sovereignty and California's environment," he said.   Jeff ⁠Merkley, a Democratic senator from Oregon, called the bill "a bad deal."   
   "It opens the gates to a flood of natural gas for data centers while leaving expanded transmission of renewable energy subject to Trump's obstruction," he said on X.   In a recent social media post, President Trump urged Congress to approve the bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE."   Julia Simon contributed reporting to this story.

                Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Nov. 16.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who has defended President Trump's war with Iran, said Friday that he opposes tying government funding to an end to the conflict as Congress struggles to avert a shutdown before Christmas.   "We're not going to shut down the war. That is President Trump's power. He's exercising his constitutional authority," Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, told Morning Edition.   Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to keep federal agencies operating, giving Democrats leverage in the Republican-controlled Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to advance. But both parties face divisions. Democrats disagree over whether to use the funding deadline to force an end to the war, while Republicans are weighing bipartisan negotiations against a party-line approach to securing additional military spending.   
   Johnson said Republicans would prefer to negotiate a spending agreement with Democrats rather than use budget reconciliation, a procedure that could allow them to approve defense funding without Democratic support.   
   "I think we'll give them one more chance," he said, referring to negotiations before the Thanksgiving recess.   Johnson, who previously supported military aid to Ukraine but later opposed additional funding, warned that temporary spending measures would hinder military modernization and weapons procurement. He pointed to the changing nature of warfare in Ukraine as an example.   A shutdown could furlough hundreds of thousands of federal workers or delay their pay just weeks before Christmas. Johnson said he hoped to avoid one but warned that Republicans would need Democratic support.   
   The war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran has killed thousands of people, threatened U.S. military bases across the region and become a point of contention in the American midterm elections. Asked what he wanted to see happen in Iran, Johnson said he hoped Iranians would rise up against their government and that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.   "I want to see the Ayatollahs on the dustbin of history," he said.   Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

title: Trump to hold press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
description: In a pool photograph distributed by the
body:
In a pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and President Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on Thursday.
                
                    Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump is set to hold a White House press conference today at noon, following his return to Washington after a four-day trip to Asia, where he sat down for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.   Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.   Watch the 12 p.m. ET news conference live:   
   The U.S. president said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.   Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.   While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.   "The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."   
   Foreign trips are often largely about the pomp and circumstance involved in meetings between heads of state. Among other special events, Trump's arrival in China, for example, included a military flyover and young dancers.   
   But the events are also extensively choreographed, with aides working months in advance to lock down agreements and commitments that the leaders can point to as evidence of a successful trip. That did not appear to be a main objective for this visit.   For Xi, he was able to boast of China's global leadership by bringing together the world's greatest nuclear powers to discuss global challenges.   For Putin, the meeting allowed a chance to reestablish Russia as a great geopolitical power on par with China and the U.S.   And for Trump, it's a chance to turn the page and demonstrate his ongoing power at a time when he's been weakened domestically after the devastating midterm elections.   In his opening remarks alongside Xi and Putin, Trump said the three leaders were making history and that they had a responsibility to the rest of the world to maintain open and respectful dialogue.   "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite," Trump said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech."   
   But while the kind words and pats on the back were prevalent, the lack of deliverables was also noteworthy.   
   It has raised questions about Trump's approach to foreign policy.   Trump has spent much of the last few years trying to replace the postwar rules-based order, ripping up traditional alliances in favor of a more personal approach to diplomacy. He prefers to work out deals personally with the world's superpowers.   But the visit may be demonstrating that access does not always produce results.   Xi and Putin have their own strategic objectives, which are not going to change because they're friendly with Trump. As Maloney put it, they also have to calculate whether agreements reached with Trump can survive domestic scrutiny or a change of administration in the coming years.   "I think both Putin and Xi recognized that President Trump's time is beginning to wane," Maloney said, "that his command of U.S. politics is also beginning to wane, and they're going to be looking to who and what may be coming next."

title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
body:
Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19.
                
                    Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.   
   Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority.    Myanmar's military-backed government on Friday dismissed the court's ruling as "unfair," according to The Associated Press. Khine Khine Soe, a spokeswoman for President Min Aung Hlaing, was quoted saying that Myanmar would make its position known after reviewing the court's decision.   Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.   
   But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.   "I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."   Genocidal campaign    For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.   The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attend a public hearing ahead of the reading of the court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, in The Hague on Thursday.
                
                    Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.   "Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."   She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."   
   Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."   "We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."   Rejected defense   Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.   
   "The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on Thursday.
                
                    Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.   
   She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.   "Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.   The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.   A group long denied recognition   In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.   Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.   
   The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.    But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.    
   In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.   
   Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.    U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."   The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.   However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.   The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.   
   Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.   Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.   Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.   
   "Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.   She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.   Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.

   🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.   Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.   
   🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.   The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.   🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.

                Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes.
                
                    Claire Harbage/NPR

   Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes. He reflects on his life, both in and out of his iconic roles, and the unexpected twists he's encountered.   🎵 Music: On Graceland Way, singer-songwriter and harpist Mikaela Davis blends psychedelic and alternative country, showcasing her boundary-pushing harp play.   🎮 Gaming: After years of waiting, fans can now revel in the Bonnie-and-Clyde love story in Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is poised to steal the crown as the biggest entertainment launch ever with up to $5 billion in projected first-week sales, according to estimates.   ❓ Quiz: What a week! title: 'Bigger than Barack Obama's election': Scholars reflect on Mississippi Senate race
description:
Transcript
        
    TONYA MOSLEY, HOST:  This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. In the final weeks of Mississippi's Senate
body:
Transcript
        
    TONYA MOSLEY, HOST:  This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. In the final weeks of Mississippi's Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom showed up outside a Donald Trump rally for his opponent and started talking to voters waiting to get in. He spent more than a year traveling across Mississippi, trying to convince people he could win, and last week, he did. Three years earlier, his opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, had blocked Colom's nomination to become a federal judge. Now he's headed to Washington to take her seat in the Senate.But there's a much longer history behind the victory. Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, descended from an enslaved woman. He's now the state's first Black U.S. senator in nearly a hundred and fifty years. It's a remarkable moment in a state where Black political power was once built, then violently dismantled in the years after Reconstruction. During the Great Migration, generations of Black Americans, including my family, fled Mississippi to escape Jim Crow and racial terror. Others, like Colom's family, stayed and fought for change.My guests today are two sons of Mississippi who have spent their lives examining the place they call home. Eddie Glaude is a professor of African American studies at Princeton University and grew up in Moss Point, a small town on the state's Gulf Coast. So I'm saying all that to say that my mother's critique has always been that Black people vote Democrat, and we don't have great candidates running. And I will say, I don't know anybody who's more critical of Mississippi politicians than Mary Coleman, my mother. And when I - and actually, when I knew he was going to win, it was when my mother looked at that man in a hoodie, and she was like, that's a Mississippi senator. This is the same mama who told me never wear a hoodie.(LAUGHTER)LAYMON: Ever.MOSLEY: I'm just thinking about, as we step out more broadly and thinking about the historic first, 'cause Colom is part of an election filled with historic firsts. Voters turned out and elected, of course, Colom, but a Hispanic governor in Texas, a Black woman governor in Georgia, a Native American woman governor in New Mexico. But we're also a country that has spent the last few years arguing about identity politics and political correctness and diversity. We have leaders in the Democratic Party who say the path forward is to not focus on identity politics. Eddie, what do you think these victories tell us?GLAUDE: Look, what happened in the South has everything to do with the fact that Black folk turned out in historic numbers without Obama on the ticket. Think about what happened in Texas, y'all. It wasn't some Black celebrity on the ballot. And Black folk in Texas turned out in historic numbers and voted for Hinojosa. And then you think about what happened in North Carolina, what happened in South Carolina, what happened in Georgia, what happened in Louisiana, what happened in Florida, and part of what I'm suggesting here is to kind of reduce that turnout to a return-to-identity politics is condescending. It's enraging, alright? You have Black voters engaging in the process in light of their interest. That is to say, you had Republicans who sought to disenfranchise us, to throw us back to the 1950s. We organized in defense of our democratic rights and in response to the assault on our economic and material conditions. I mean, and so to reduce that to identity, politics - right? - reveals - how can I put this in a delicate way? Well, let's not be delicate.LAYMON: (Laughter).GLAUDE: The Democratic Party all too often thinks of Black voters as cattle chewing cud...LAYMON: Yep.GLAUDE: ...To be herded every two and four years as if we're not a constituency that has interest. You know, Baldwin used to loathe this question - what else does the Negro want? And Baldwin would say, if you thought of me as a human being, you would know exactly what I want. I want the exact same things you do for your babies, right? So I think it's a red herring. That's the short answer. I think that the worry about identity politics is a red herring. But you need to speak to the conditions of a constituency that fundamentally just handed the Congress to you.MOSLEY: Let's take a short break. If you're just joining us, my guests are Princeton scholar Eddie Glaude and Rice University professor Kiese Laymon. We'll be right back after a short break. This is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MOSLEY: This is FRESH AIR. And today, I am talking with Eddie Glaude and Kiese Laymon about Scott Colom's historic Senate election win in Mississippi.Colom's campaign got a lot of attention for its humorous ads, but he closed with a very different ad filmed in Jackson at the home of Medgar Evers, who was the NAACP leader who was assassinated in his own driveway back in 1963. And I just want to play it. Let's listen.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)COLOM: There's a house in Jackson every Mississippian ought to walk through once. It looks like every other house on the street, except for it isn't.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)COLOM: It has no front door. You come in through the carport, where the walls give you some cover. The children slept on the floor below the windows. Their father taught them that if they ever heard gunfire, they should crawl to the bathroom. He made it a game.I've been a prosecutor for 10 years. Unfortunately, I've stood in a lot of houses where something terrible happened. This isn't any house. This isn't any tragedy.(SOUNDBITE OF CAMERA FLASH)COLOM: This is where Medgar Evers died. He fought for this country in Normandy.(SOUNDBITE OF CAMERA FLASH)COLOM: He came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn't let him vote.(SOUNDBITE OF CAMERA FLASH)COLOM: So he organized, helping other people register. Just after midnight on June 12, 1963, he pulled into here with an arm full of T-shirts that said, Jim Crow must go. A man hiding across the street shot him in the back.(SOUNDBITE OF CAMERA FLASH)COLOM: Two juries let that man walk. His wife, Myrlie...(SOUNDBITE OF CAMERA FLASH)COLOM: ...Never stopped. It took 31 years, then a Mississippi prosecutor reopened the case, and a Mississippi jury, both Black and white, convicted him. In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection. He was killed for helping Mississippians vote. On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.MOSLEY: That was one of the last ads before the election of Scott Colom. And you could hear those flashes. Those were photo flashes. That ad made me think about - we keep hearing people call this victory a political miracle. But this ad is a reminder that, in a way, calling it a miracle misses the people who made it possible. What does it make you guys think about?LAYMON: Well, I can just say, you know, I - for four years that I went to high school, I went to - you had to drive every day Medgar Evers Boulevard. My mother's mentor, Margaret Walker, lived a few streets over from Medgar Evers. We used to play football right in front of Medgar Evers' house. And it's not one of these situations where we never know who Medgar Evers was. Like, to us, Medgar Evers wanted the best for Black Mississippians, and he wanted the best for Mississippi. And that is why he was shot.So hearing Scott in his campaign with that ad, when the tone of the campaign - right? - had been so lifted with the pick a protein, pick another senator ad, one, I think, speaks to the daring, and I think whether or not we know it or not, speaks to Scott and his people's desire to connect his ability to govern to historic Black activists of the past. Now, whether or not that is a good idea, as far as governance goes, I'm not sure, right? Because Medgar Evers had a different role to play than Scott does I believe. But what I love about it is that it animates, like, a reality for Mississippians. Medgar Evers, like, we - that's our street. His house is where we - you know, we play ball there. And it makes me remember that, like, we grew up living what people call history. And I think that can be very important for young people trying to find some sense of self in this nation.GLAUDE: Right, it was the closing ad of the campaign that suggested or presented or projected the fact that the campaign itself carried the weight of history itself. When I saw it, I was trying to process it in a number of different ways. And, ironically, you know, Kiese, I reached for Faulkner and "Requiem For A Nun," that line, you know, the past is never dead. It's not even past, right? And so there was this sense in which the invocation of Medgar Evers in that moment is to not just simply recall a horrific act of murder, right? But to bring it into the present in a way such that it can inform and shape our choices in very clear and concrete ways.MOSLEY: Colom won by exactly 8,031 votes. And I'm thinking about the last time a Black man went to the Senate for the state of Mississippi - a very long time ago. It was undone - that progress during Reconstruction - undone within a generation. What are you both watching for this time?LAYMON: Wow. I mean, honestly, because we're talking to y'all, I'm watching for and hoping for immense health and safety to come to Scott Colom and his wife, Nadia, and their incredible children. None of this is possible unless we keep them safe. I wish this wasn't something we had to say. This is something we have to say. So I have no doubt that that man is going to go out there and push and make a path for more potential young folks who have his gumption to lead Mississippi. I just know that in a state that has taken this long to change, the movement from Candidate Colom to Senator Colom has to be taken seriously, and he has to be protected along the way.And similarly, I will just say, as someone who loves Mississippi, I expect Scott Colom to risk for all of the Mississippi's children. Scott Colom is not an artist. He's not a writer. He can't say things we can say. When I say all of Mississippi's children, I'm talking about all of Mississippi's children - the queer children, the poor children, the trans children. I think his role was made possible because of radical interventions from folks like Fannie Lou Hamer. I don't know how much radical intervention we can expect from a senator, but I expect Scott Colom, while keeping himself and his family safe, to also keep all children of Mississippi safe by all means necessary or to attempt to. And I think that will lead to this being not just the first, but the first of a real, sustained movement for love, progress and connectivity in Mississippi.GLAUDE: Yeah. Yeah, that's it. You know, I pray that he doesn't fall for the siren song of Washington, D.C.MOSLEY: Oh.LAYMON: Yeah. Yeah.GLAUDE: You know, Washington, D.C., offers, you know, all sorts of temptations about the nature of power, about what it means to be the first and the like. I hope he takes that gift of Mississippi that orients us in a certain sort of way to the world. I hope he brings it to Washington, D.C., and he lets all of them see it for what it is and all of its power. I know that's being abstract, but that has everything to do with, I think, the power of what it means to be from this place. That's the first thing.The second thing, I think, you know, politicians inevitably disappoint. I learned that early on. But I want to see what Cassandra Welchlin and Rukia Lumumba and...LAYMON: Yeah.GLAUDE: ...Sister Lambright-Haynes and all of those organizers on the ground who made this possible - I want to see what they do in holding Scott Colom accountable. I can't wait to continue to see what they do, and how Scott plays this role in that effort.LAYMON: Yes. I agree with Eddie. I mean, I hope - and if there's any moment where Democrats could learn that you must follow the people, it is this moment. And I hope that the Democrats - you follow the people by funding the people but also being open to the people's visions. And I have absolute trust in that group of people that helped Scott get elected. I have no doubt in my mind that their vision for Mississippi is the vision for Mississippi and actually the vision for this nation and the world. Whether the Democratic Party sees that or not is something else. But...GLAUDE: (Laughter).LAYMON: ...It's right there. It's right there for you.MOSLEY: Kiese Laymon and Eddie Glaude, thank you so much for this conversation.GLAUDE: Thank you.LAYMON: Thank you so much for giving us space.MOSLEY: Eddie Glaude is a professor of African American Studies at Princeton University and the author of several books, including "Begin Again" and "America, U.S.A." Kiese Laymon is a professor of English and creative writing at Rice University and the author of the acclaimed memoir, "Heavy." His new memoir, "Good, God: A Creation Story," will be published this spring.(SOUNDBITE OF DEEP BLUE ORGAN TRIO'S "YOU HAVEN'T DONE NOTHIN'")MOSLEY: If you'd like to catch up on interviews you've missed, like our conversation with LeVar Burton about his new memoir or Lynn Novick about her new documentary on crime and punishment in America, check out our podcast. You'll find lots of FRESH AIR interviews. You can also watch some of our interviews on our YouTube page, thisisfreshair.FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director and engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Roberta Shorrock, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Susan Nyakundi, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler. Our digital media producer is Molly Seavy-Nesper. Thea Chaloner directed today's show. With Terry Gross, I'm Tonya Mosley.(SOUNDBITE OF DEEP BLUE ORGAN TRIO'S "YOU HAVEN'T DONE NOTHIN'")

title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
description: Federal judges have issued temporary res
body:
Federal judges have issued temporary restraining orders to block construction of Trump's arch and keep East Potomac Park open.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.   D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.   
   Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.   "The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.   The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.   That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.   In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.   
   "This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.   Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.   Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch.
                
                    Tom Brenner/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/AP
    

   
   The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.   
   In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.   In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."   
   White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.   Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.   'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac    Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.   Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.   
   But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.   Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.   
   On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.   Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.   The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                National Park Service employees walk past a golfer at East Potomac Park on Monday, after a judge ordered the administration to keep the park open.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.   Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.   The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).   
   Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.   Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.   Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.   Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.   Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.   Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.   "In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.   
   Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."   "Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"   Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.    Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

title: New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
description: New York City officials have created a r
body:
New York City officials have created a road map for how they'll close the jail complex on Rikers Island and move to smaller facilities within the boroughs. Mayor Zohran Mamdani closed the North Infirmary Command building, seen here, on Rikers earlier this year.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.   "It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."   Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.   
   Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.   Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.   But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Empty cells at the Rikers Island jail complex in New York City on Nov. 18, 2026. The city's plan to close Rikers aims to transform the conditions inside the city's jails and lower their population.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   The plan — which takes on both the conditions inside the jails and the size of the population behind bars — is ambitious. It seeks to transform how the city government thinks about crime prevention and safety overall, says Insha Rahman, president of the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit.   "If New York City can do this at scale, which it will, it is encouragement for places like LA, like Chicago, like Philadelphia, like Houston to do the same," Rahman says.   A goal set by the city years ago   In 2019, the New York City Council approved a plan to close Rikers by 2027, and to build in its place four smaller jails in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx.   
   Rikers is on an island between Queens and the Bronx, out of sight for many New Yorkers. The borough-based jails will be closer to the courts and to public transit, making it easier for families, lawyers and service providers to visit people inside the facilities.   Since 2019, not a lot of progress has been made toward closing Rikers. City officials acknowledge they won't make the 2027 deadline. But Mamdani says the city is in a new moment.   "We're not the first administration to talk about this. We also know that the last administration had no interest in advancing this," Mamdani told NPR. "And we are also confident that we can be the first administration to deliver on it."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
                Mayor Zohran Mamdani greets New York City Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards on Sept. 4, 2026. Mamdani appointed Richards earlier this year to lead the department.Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office
                
                    Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office
                
                hide caption
    
        Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office
    

   
   Earlier this year, he appointed a "Close Rikers Czar" dedicated to closing the jail and reducing the jail population. The mayor also appointed Stanley Richards as commissioner of the DOC, the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department.   Mamdani says his administration has already taken concrete steps: The city revived plans for a housing initiative for New Yorkers released from jail with medical needs, for instance, and it opened a therapeutic housing unit at a public hospital in Manhattan.   'Human dignity at the center of incarceration'   Last year, a federal judge stripped the city of its authority over Rikers. Operations are now controlled by a remediation manager, who released his own initial plan earlier this year for bringing the jail system into legal compliance, independent of the city's plan.   Aspects of that plan took inspiration from carceral systems in Europe, a growing trend among correctional leaders across the U.S. The remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, traveled with Commissioner Richards to Germany earlier this year on a trip organized by the Vera Institute. There, they observed the country's prisons and jails, which are often regarded as an international model.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Staff walk in a prison courtyard in Berlin, Germany. The prison system in the country is often regarded as an international model, focusing on human dignity for people in custody.
                
                    Lena Mucha
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Lena Mucha
    

   
   "While German correctional systems are not directly transferable to New York, they reflect a fundamentally different orientation — one that places human dignity at the center of incarceration," Deml wrote in his plan.   
   Last month, the Vera Institute took a second group of New Yorkers to Germany to see how jails can look when they're done right, including the Moabit jail in Berlin. Each member of that group had a part to play in reimagining New York City's criminal justice system: a prosecutor, a judge, a city councilmember, the chief who supervises officers at Rikers, among others.   At first glance, the group observed, Moabit looked like a lot of jails in the U.S., but key differences emerged on closer inspection. The jail was quiet. The cells had windows to the outside. In some of them, a door inside connected it to the adjacent cell.   "Some people are afraid of the first night here, and sometimes it really helps just to open the door to have someone to talk to," Katharina Spanaus, a staff member at Moabit, told the group.   There were also televisions in the cells to calm people down, and in the hallway, a vending machine selling cigarettes.   "I'll never forget the cigarette vending machine," says Christopher Watler, who was recently appointed chair of the New York City Board of Correction, which oversees the city's jail system.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Christopher Watler, who recently became chair of the New York City Board of Correction, the independent body responsible for overseeing the city's jail system, was struck in Germany by the humanity baked into the country's jail system.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   What struck him wasn't really the cigarettes, but what the gesture communicates about treating people as human, Watler says.   It also showed him how far New York City has to go.   Just a week earlier, he sat at his first board meeting in New York, where he heard stories that evoked a different image. At the start, the board listened to anonymous phone calls from people held at Rikers.   The callers voiced concerns: A woman reported black mold. A man said he was denied his medications. Another pleaded for a less violent environment.   "New York City's a great city. Our jail system isn't great," Watler says. "It's a broken thing. But how do you repair broken things?"   
   'The sum of all the efforts will help'   The four new jails won't be fully completed for another six years. Each facility will have more access to natural light and fresh air, and more space for recreation, vocational training and education.   Together, the new jails will hold about 2,000 fewer people than the approximately 6,600 people Rikers holds now.   The city's plan invests more than $250 million across the next several years in efforts to reduce the number of people in jail, for instance, by expanding alternatives to incarceration like diversion programs and electronic monitoring.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Construction continues on the new Brooklyn-based jail, one of four being built by the city to replace Rikers. The site is due to be completed in 2029.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   It also aims to keep people from committing crimes, by expanding services like supportive housing and mental health treatment.   Another way to lower a jail's population is to shorten how long people stay there. The average length of stay of people in New York City DOC custody was nearly twice as long in 2025 as it was in 2015, according to the policy journal Vital City.   The vast majority of people at Rikers are awaiting trial, and many of their cases take longer to process than national standards dictate. Nearly a quarter have been in jail for more than a year.   Judge Joseph Zayas, chief administrative judge of the New York State Unified Court System, told NPR there are many factors that can lengthen a jail stay, including processing evidence during discovery and administering mental health assessments, for instance.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
                Judge Joseph Zayas, chief administrative judge of the New York State Unified Court System, says many factors can delay a court case, which is one of the contributing factors to Rikers' population size.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   "The only way to solve this backlog problem is to hit each of these things. The sum of all of the efforts will help," Zayas says.   The city is planning a task force dedicated to speeding up court cases, but the forces affecting that are outside city hall's control. Judges act independently from the mayor, as do district attorneys. City officials say they are investing in those relationships.   'If you are wrong, then you have crowded jails'   Some people, including those with deep knowledge of Rikers, are concerned with what happens if the city doesn't lower the jail population enough.   
   Vincent Schiraldi, who was DOC commissioner under Mayor Bill de Blasio, says he can understand that.   "It's really hard to have the guts to forecast lower incarceration numbers. Because if you are wrong, then you have crowded jails and you're in trouble," says Schiraldi, who now runs a philanthropic fund to close Rikers.   Other cities have dramatically reduced their jail populations. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, New Orleans reduced its jail population by more than two thirds in the decade after.   Schiraldi pointed out that aside from an increase during the pandemic, crime rates have trended downward for decades.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A single jail cell as construction continues on the Brooklyn detention center, one of four being built by the city to replace Rikers. Some people with knowledge of the city's criminal justice system are worried that the city doesn't have a back-up plan if it can't lower the jail population enough to fit the new borough-based jails.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   If crime increases again, Schiraldi says, "Then we deal with it. What is the scenario by which the government spends billions of dollars just in case?"   But Elizabeth Glazer, who led the Office of Criminal Justice under de Blasio, told NPR she hopes the mayor will be pragmatic when it comes to having contingency plans – including the possibility of building again on Rikers Island.   She says it is possible to shrink the jail population, but it's not going to be easy.   "It requires relentless attention, coordination and organization around a common goal to get it done," says Glazer, who is also the founder of Vital City. "Even if you hit that number, the question is, can that be sustained for the decades when all you have is that capacity?"   Still, for some people the city's plan is a crucial opportunity, after years of inaction have left thousands of people held at the jail under inhumane conditions.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Tina Luongo, who leads the criminal defense practice at the Legal Aid Society, speaks during a rally to protest a death on Rikers Island at City Hall on Oct. 25, 2022 in New York City. Luongo says the city's new plan represents an opportunity to move forward, after years of inaction have left thousands of people jailed on Rikers in inhumane conditions.
                
                    Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
    

   
   "We wait for these perfect plans, and for all the reasons we know, including funding, those perfect plans never come to pass. And so what do we do? We do nothing," says Tina Luongo, who leads the criminal defense practice at the Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action lawsuit that resulted in the remediation manager's appointment.   
   Changing the culture at Rikers   Officials caution the new jails alone won't solve the systemic problems at Rikers.   Over the last decade, the federal government has documented a "culture of violence" among the guards. In 2023, more than 700 women sued the city alleging they'd been raped or sexually abused by staff at Rikers, according to a Gothamist investigation.   "People talk about culture change and that's really just a euphemism for the extraordinary brutality and violence that has plagued Rikers," Glazer says. "If you're going to move the very same system into the new buildings, you're going to move the problem of violence as well."   In their report, city officials outline plans for more training and mentoring for staff, tighter oversight, and more programming for people in jail.   Commissioner Richards told NPR he wants to see the jail's culture transform and become more like what he saw in Germany, where human dignity is non-negotiable for everyone. That includes staff, who Richards says have been demonized.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Stanley Richards, commissioner of the New York City Department of Correction, sits in an empty jail cell in the Rikers Island complex on Nov. 18, 2026. Richards is the first formerly incarcerated person to have been appointed to the role.
                
                    Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR
    

   
   "Part of the work that I'm doing is showing value and appreciation to our staff. So they begin to expand their capacity to show that same value and humanity to the people who come to us," Richards says.   But he didn't offer specifics on what exactly will change. That may be in part because he has a more immediate focus: safety and security.   The plan set forth by Deml, the remediation manager, starts with the most basic correctional functions, including protocols for securing doors. Richards, who was incarcerated at Rikers himself 40 years ago, says they need to start somewhere.   "Everybody wants something to happen by tomorrow. And we are in a moment of urgency. But it takes time to turn," he says.   The larger goal remains the same: for the failures of Rikers to not be carried into the next generation of New York City jails.

title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
description: With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.   Some 56
body:
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.   Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.   It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.   
   Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.   Nearly 50 House seats flipped   So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.   That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.   It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.   
   The biggest House majority in a generation   This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.   If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.   
   Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.   This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.   Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.
